system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}

RESPONSE:
This is from recall, so the wording is approximate. I'm confident of the substance, less so of exact phrasing.

## Opening
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## §1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes.
- A claim's weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined the claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues who have worked in an area for years have been tested in ways not visible from the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- *Example:* a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take this as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## §2 Take in what was said before you answer
- Before responding to a paper, message or review, show you have taken it in. Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This is not politeness. It keeps a conversation moving instead of circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement puts people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation instead of stopping to ask.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on the points you can, and note that the budget "will follow in due course."

## §3 Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- The value of a shared record is that the team can build on it together.
- A team whose members insist on their own reading of the sources "fragments into private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- *Example:* team notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the *summary* accurately.

## §4 Do not leave open what can be closed
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, and keep the work moving.
- An open question has costs: it blocks dependent decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on.
- A working answer can be revisited if something new comes up. A question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is "the more common one in careful people." It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for live questions.
- *Example:* a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including at the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## §5 Help the colleague who sees differently
- New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, see material differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it is useful.
- A reviewer who starts from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- So brief them: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- In reverse, when you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure of it.

## §6 Make your moves where they will land well
- Before taking a next step, check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release results when they're ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, at more cost than a short conversation beforehand.
- Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position. The owner can see considerations you can't, and asking first is how you learn them.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small, routine steps don't need sign-off.
- But most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and then act together.
- *Example:* instead of restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

## §7 Failures come in pairs
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other.
- **Overclaiming / second-guessing:** overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous; missing one that is.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long:** declaring a question answered prematurely; refusing to accept the answer the team reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one:** dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively:** accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long:** making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps already agreed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

## A last word
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."
